'''William Carragan''' (July 18, 1937 – June 9, 2024) was an American musicologist particularly known for his research into the music of [[Anton Bruckner]]. He spent many years producing a completion of Bruckner's [[Symphony No. 9 (Bruckner)|Ninth Symphony]].

== Education and career in physics==
Born in Troy, New York, Carragan learned physics from his father George Howard Carragan (1896–1982, a physics professor) and music from his mother Martha Beck (1900–1997, a pianist and composer of educational pieces for children who knew [[Sergei Rachmaninoff]]).<ref>[https://carragan.com/martha-beck/ Martha Beck archive]</ref> He also took piano lessons with [[Albany, New York|Albany]] pianist Stanley Hummel (1908–2005), and later further piano lessons with [[Gilbert Kalish]], also studying harpsichord with Louis Bagger. 

But following his father he became a physicist and professor at [[Hudson Valley Community College]] for 35 years, from 1965 until 2001. While there he published a comprehensive four-volume textbook of introductory university physics.<ref name=tu/>

== Bruckner Editions ==
As a musicologist, Carragan's primary concerns were analytical aspects of the music, and history, of the performances of Bruckner's symphonies. He was a contributing editor of the Bruckner Collected Edition in Vienna, sponsored by the [[International Bruckner Society]]. For the Collected Edition, at the request of [[Leopold Nowak]], Carragan prepared a new edition of Bruckner's [[Symphony No. 2 (Bruckner)|Second Symphony]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Symphony No. 2 in C Minor|url=http://www.mwv.at/english/TextBruckner/Katalog/symph02.htm|website=Musikwissenschaftlicher Verlag}}</ref><ref>''Anton Bruckner: Sämtliche Werke: Band II: II. Symphonie c-Moll'', Musikwissenschaftlicher Verlag der Internationalen Bruckner-Gesellschaft, Vienna -  II/1: '' Fassung 1872'', William Carragan (editor), 2005; II/2: '' Fassung 1877'', new edition by William Carragan, 2007</ref> in two versions (1872 and 1877), as well as  the 1883 and 1886 variants of the Symphony.<ref>[https://carragan.com/composer-anton-bruckner/second-symphony-studies/the-early-version-of-bruckners-second-symphony/ The Early Version of Bruckner’s Second Symphony]</ref> 

Carragan reconstructed for the first time the first version of Bruckner's [[Symphony No. 1 (Bruckner)|First]] (1866),<ref>{{cite web|title=Editors and Authors|url=http://www.mwv.at/english/TextLeftFrame/heraus.htm#05|website=Musikwissenschaftlicher Verlag}}</ref><ref name="Symphony No. 1 conducted by Georg Tintner00">{{cite journal| last= McColley |first= Robert |title= Symphony No. 1 conducted by Georg Tintner |journal = Fanfare |volume=24 |pages=1 | date= September 1, 2000 |url= http://www.fanfarearchive.com}}</ref> the previously unheard versions of the [[Symphony No. 3 (Bruckner)|Third]] from 1874 and 1876,<ref>[https://carragan.com/composer-anton-bruckner/a-new-version-of-the-third-symphony/, A New Version of the Third Symphony]</ref><ref>Symphony No. 3 (1876 version) - Richard Pittman with the New England Philharmonic - Live, 2 March  2019: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Wntw_Uu0dJs  I. Gemässigt, mehr bewegt, Misterioso], [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GN2KFtL_Pc8 II. Adagio, Bewegt, quasi Andante, feierlich], [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4MVmwkeLG3E III. Ziemlich schnell], [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BT6v_Ut5fEE IV. Finale, Allegro])</ref> and of the [[Symphony No. 4 (Bruckner)|Fourth]] from 1878, as well as the 1888 intermediate versions of the [[Symphony No. 8 (Bruckner)|Eighth]].<ref>[https://carragan.com/composer-anton-bruckner/bruckners-eighth-a-work-in-progress/ Bruckner’s Eighth Symphony as a Work in Progress]</ref> He also devoted himself to completing Bruckner's [[Symphony No. 9 (Bruckner)|Ninth]] symphony.<ref name="MUSIC: COMPLETING BRUCKNER'S NINTH">{{cite news|last= Rothstein |first=Edward |title=MUSIC: COMPLETING BRUCKNER'S NINTH|work=New York Times|date=January 9, 1984|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1984/01/09/arts/music-completing-bruckner-s-ninth.html}}</ref> That completion has been widely performed and recorded,<ref>{{in lang|fr}} [https://sites.google.com/site/letocartsebastien/accueil-francais/bruckner-symphonie9-finale Notes on the completion of the Finale of the Ninth Symphony of Bruckner] by Sébastien Letocart.</ref> the most recently in a revised version from 2017. 

Carragan published ''Anton Bruckner: Eleven Symphonies'' – a "Red Book" on the different versions of Bruckner's Symphonies issued by the Bruckner Society of America.<ref>[https://brucknerredbook.com/the-red-book/ The Bruckner Red Book]</ref> He served as consultant in many performances of Bruckner symphonies.<ref name="Carragan - Berky interview on Bruckner's 7th Symphony">{{cite interview|last=Berky |first= John |title=Carragan - Berky interview on Bruckner's 7th Symphony |date=November 17, 2011| url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kgSCROLAvV8}}</ref> In 1991 he was accorded the Gold-Plakette of the Brucknerbund Oberösterreich, and in 2010 he was awarded the Kilenyi Medal of Honor of the Bruckner Society of America.

== Other work ==
For the [[Franz Schubert]] anniversary of 1978, Carragan completed and performed several of Schubert's unfinished piano sonatas, and ten years later he prepared a four-movement version of the Schubert's [[Symphony No. 8 (Schubert)|Eighth]] symphony which was recorded in Germany with the [[Philharmonie Festiva]].<ref name="Philharmonie Festiva">{{cite news|last=Music|first=Ebracht|title=PHILHARMONIE FESTIVA|work=Mainpost|date=January 1, 2016|url=http://www.ebracher-musiksommer.de/philharmonie-festiva|access-date=March 30, 2017|archive-date=September 15, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180915212334/http://www.ebracher-musiksommer.de/philharmonie-festiva|url-status=dead}}</ref>

With respect to the baroque era, Carragan made arrangements of a concerto for four violins by [[Antonio Vivaldi]], Op. 3, no. 1, for four harpsichords, as well as a concerto for two violins, Op. 3, no. 8, arranged after J.S. Bach for two harpsichords.<ref>[http://www.vintageperformance.com/cdh/william_carragan.htm Presentation of Carragan]</ref>

==Personal life and death==
Carragan married Julia Weston Faunce in April 1966.<ref>[https://www.nytimes.com/1966/02/23/archives/julia-faunce-engaged-to-william-carragan.htmlhttps://www.nytimes.com/1966/02/23/archives/julia-faunce-engaged-to-william-carragan.html 'Julia Faunce Engaged To William Carragan' in ''The New York Times'', 23 February 1966, p. 32]</ref> She was a teacher and medieval historian who also taught at Hudson Valley College for 34 years. He retired in 2000 to care for his wife, who died of cancer in 2001. For the last two decades of his life he lived in the [[Brunswick, New York|Brunswick]] home of his childhood.<ref name=tu/> He was also a cantor at Saint George Antiochian Orthodox Church in Albany, NY. 

Carragan died following a stroke on June 9, 2024, at the age of 86.<ref name=tu>Steve Barnes, [https://www.timesunion.com/news/article/william-carragan-troy-hvcc-obituary-bruckner-19509418.php 'Troy physicist and musicologist William Carragan dies at 86'], ''Times Union'', June 12, 2024</ref><ref>[https://www.abruckner.com/editorsnote/features/william-carragan-1937-2024/ William Carragan (1937-2024)]</ref>
